moduleTitle: SQE1 · Wills and Administration of Estates
title: Inheritance tax I: the nil-rate bands and exemptions
subtitle: The NRB, the transferable NRB, the residence NRB and its taper, and the main lifetime and death exemptions
objectives: State the nil-rate band and residence nil-rate band, and explain how each transfers between spouses and civil partners
Explain how the residence nil-rate band tapers away for larger estates
Apply the spouse, charity, annual, small gifts, and normal expenditure out of income exemptions to a fact pattern to calculate the tax-free threshold available to an estate

leadingAuthorities.role: Transferable nil-rate band between spouses and civil partners
Downsizing addition rules preserving the residence nil-rate band where the qualifying home has been sold
Spouse/civil partner, charity, annual, small gifts, and normal expenditure exemptions

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often learn '£325,000, tax-free' as a fixed fact and stop there. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the headline figure — this lesson is about the bands and exemptions that change what an estate actually pays.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've got the definitions down. The test pool leans on scenario arithmetic — expect to combine a transferable NRB, a residence NRB, and an exemption in the same question.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about which band is which — the NRB and RNRB are easy to conflate, and the rest of the lesson depends on keeping them separate.

overview.hook: Every estate has a tax-free amount before inheritance tax bites — but almost no estate actually has just one. A married couple's second-to-die estate can carry across two nil-rate bands, two residence nil-rate bands, and a set of exemptions that were never used the first time round. Getting the threshold right, rather than reaching for the headline £325,000 figure, is often the single biggest lever a private client solicitor has.
overview.lawStatedNotice: The nil-rate band and residence nil-rate band are frozen cash figures set by government and reviewed periodically rather than indexed automatically — they can and do change at the Budget. A reform to business and agricultural relief announced for 2026 is a live example of how quickly the wider IHT landscape can move; always check the current figures and rules before advising, rather than relying on any figure quoted here as fixed.

parts.heading: The nil-rate band: one figure, frozen for years
parts.voice: direct — sets the baseline before complicating it
body: Every individual's estate on death benefits from a nil-rate band (NRB) — a slice of the estate charged to inheritance tax at 0% before the standard 40% rate applies to the rest. The NRB has been frozen at the same cash figure for an unusually long stretch of years, which matters practically: as asset values (particularly property) rise, more estates are pulled above a threshold that isn't moving with them.

The NRB is set by s 7 and Schedule 1 IHTA 1984 and is reviewed periodically by government rather than uprated automatically each year. A solicitor advising on an estate should always check the figure current at the date of death, not assume it matches an earlier transaction or an earlier exam question.
On its own, the NRB is a modest planning tool. Its real power in practice comes from being transferable between spouses and civil partners — the subject of the next part.

components.definition: The value of an individual's estate charged to inheritance tax at 0% before the standard rate applies to the remainder; a frozen cash figure set by government and periodically reviewed, not automatically indexed.

interaction.prompt: Is the nil-rate band automatically increased each year in line with inflation?
options: No — it is a frozen cash figure reviewed periodically by government
Yes — it rises automatically with the Consumer Prices Index every year
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Treat the NRB as a figure to check at the date of death, not as something that moves predictably year to year.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — the NRB has in fact been held at the same cash figure for a long period, reviewed periodically rather than automatically uprated. That freeze is exactly what makes it worth double-checking on the facts.

parts.heading: The transferable nil-rate band
parts.voice: worked-example — shows the mechanism through numbers, not just prose
body: Section 8A IHTA 1984 allows any unused percentage of a deceased spouse or civil partner's nil-rate band to transfer to the surviving spouse or civil partner's estate on the survivor's later death — even though the couple may never have discussed IHT planning at all.

The mechanism works in percentages, not cash amounts, which is what makes it robust even though the NRB figure itself may change between the two deaths. If the first spouse to die leaves everything to the survivor (using the spouse exemption, covered later in this lesson), 100% of their NRB is unused and transfers across — meaning the survivor's estate can benefit from up to double the standard NRB when they die.

Only one full uplift is possible: even with multiple earlier marriages, the maximum transferable percentage is capped at 100% of one NRB, so a survivor's estate can never benefit from more than double the standard NRB in total, however many previous spouses or civil partners predeceased them.

components.label: How the transferable NRB works
points: Governed by percentage of NRB unused, not a fixed cash sum, at the first death
Claimed on the second death by the survivor's personal representatives
Capped overall at 100% — a survivor cannot end up with more than double the standard NRB
Most commonly fully available where the first spouse left their estate to the survivor under the spouse exemption

interaction.prompt: Husband dies first, leaving his entire estate to his wife using the spouse exemption, so none of his NRB is used on his death. When his wife later dies, what NRB is potentially available to her estate?
options: Only her own single NRB — her husband's unused NRB cannot be transferred
Up to double the standard NRB, since 100% of her husband's NRB transfers across
Half of her husband's NRB only, regardless of how much he left unused
interaction.explanation: Because the husband used none of his NRB (his whole estate passed under the spouse exemption), 100% of it is available to transfer, giving the wife's estate the benefit of up to two full nil-rate bands on her later death.

parts.heading: The residence nil-rate band and its taper
parts.voice: structural — treats the RNRB as a second, conditional band with its own rules
body: Alongside the standard NRB, an additional residence nil-rate band (RNRB) applies where a qualifying residential interest — broadly, a home the deceased has lived in — is left to direct descendants (children, grandchildren, and further down the line, including step-children and adopted children). Like the standard NRB, any unused percentage transfers between spouses and civil partners.

The RNRB is not available without limit. For larger estates, it tapers away: for every £2 by which the estate's net value exceeds a set taper threshold, £1 of RNRB is lost, until it is extinguished entirely once the estate is large enough.

A special rule — the downsizing addition, under s 8FA-8FE IHTA 1984 — protects a deceased who sold or gave away a more valuable home before death and downsized (or ceased to own a home at all), so that the RNRB they would have had is not simply lost because the qualifying home no longer exists at death, provided assets of an equivalent value pass to direct descendants.

components.definition: An additional nil-rate band available where a qualifying residential interest passes to direct descendants; transferable between spouses and civil partners like the standard NRB, but tapered away for estates above a set net value threshold and extinguished above a further threshold.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that most directly triggers the downsizing addition rules.
interaction.scenarioText: Six years before her death, an elderly widow sold the four-bedroom family home she had lived in for decades and moved into a smaller flat, later leaving her estate, including the flat, to her two children.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct — selling (downsizing from) the more valuable home is exactly the situation the downsizing addition exists to address, provided assets of equivalent value pass to direct descendants like her children here.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact about giving up the more valuable property, not the fact about who eventually inherits — the downsizing addition responds to the change in what property is owned at death.

parts.heading: The exemptions: spouse, charity, annual, small gifts, normal expenditure
parts.voice: reference-style — a checklist students will return to
body: Beyond the nil-rate bands, a set of statutory exemptions can remove value from an estate, or from a lifetime gift, entirely — no tax at all, rather than merely a 0% band. These matter both for lifetime giving and on death.

The spouse or civil partner exemption (s 18) is unlimited between UK-domiciled spouses and civil partners; the charity exemption (s 23) is unlimited on gifts to qualifying charities, and leaving at least 10% of a net estate to charity can also reduce the rate on the rest of the estate. The annual exemption (s 19) allows £3,000 of lifetime gifts each tax year free of IHT, with one year's unused amount carried forward. The small gifts exemption (s 20) allows unlimited small gifts of up to £250 per recipient per tax year, provided no other exemption is used for the same recipient in the same year. Normal expenditure out of income (s 21) exempts regular gifts made out of surplus income — not capital — that do not reduce the donor's usual standard of living.

components.label: The main lifetime and death exemptions
points: Spouse/civil partner exemption (s 18) — unlimited between UK-domiciled spouses and civil partners
Charity exemption (s 23) — unlimited, and can reduce the death rate where 10%+ of the net estate passes to charity
Annual exemption (s 19) — £3,000 per tax year, with one year's unused balance carried forward
Small gifts exemption (s 20) — up to £250 per recipient per tax year, but not combinable with another exemption for the same recipient
Normal expenditure out of income (s 21) — regular gifts from surplus income that do not affect the donor's usual standard of living

interaction.prompt: A donor wants to use both the small gifts exemption and the annual exemption for a gift to the same grandchild in the same tax year. Can they combine the two exemptions for that single gift?
options: No — the small gifts exemption cannot be combined with another exemption for the same recipient in the same year
Yes — exemptions can always be stacked without limit for a single recipient
interaction.explanation: Section 20's small gifts exemption is expressly unavailable where another exemption (such as the annual exemption) is used for the same recipient in the same tax year — the donor must choose which exemption covers that particular gift.

parts.heading: Bringing it together: calculating the tax-free threshold
parts.voice: worked-example — a full calculation to consolidate the lesson
body: A private client solicitor rarely applies one band or exemption in isolation. A typical second-death estate involves stacking the deceased's own NRB, any transferred NRB, the deceased's own RNRB (checked for taper), any transferred RNRB, and then applying whatever exemptions bite before the remaining balance is taxed.

Get the order wrong — or forget that the RNRB only applies to the residential element passing to direct descendants, or that the taper applies to the whole estate's net value rather than just the home — and the calculation collapses. This is exactly the kind of multi-step arithmetic the SQE1 tests, because it rewards precision over memorised headline figures.
The next lesson builds directly on this one: even after the threshold is calculated, lifetime giving and post-death planning can still reshape what actually falls into the taxable estate.

components.title: Working out the available threshold
components.description: The order of steps for calculating an estate's tax-free amount before applying the death rate.

nodes.label: Start with the deceased's own NRB
Add any transferred NRB from a predeceasing spouse/civil partner
Add the deceased's own RNRB, if a qualifying residence passes to direct descendants
Check whether the RNRB is tapered by the estate's net value
Add any transferred RNRB from a predeceasing spouse/civil partner
Apply exemptions (spouse, charity, annual, small gifts, normal expenditure) to the remaining value

components.textAlternative: To calculate the tax-free threshold: start with the deceased's own NRB, add any transferred NRB, add the deceased's own RNRB if a qualifying residence passes to direct descendants, check whether that RNRB is tapered by the estate's net value, add any transferred RNRB, and finally apply the relevant exemptions to the remaining value before the death rate is charged on what is left.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that the RNRB taper is measured against the whole estate's net value, not just the value of the home passing to direct descendants?
sliderLabels: Taper measured against the home's value only
Taper measured against the whole estate's net value
interaction.correctPosition: Taper measured against the whole estate's net value
interaction.explanation: The taper threshold is applied to the net value of the whole estate, not merely the residential interest — a large estate can lose RNRB even if the home itself is modest, because it is the total estate value that drives the taper.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor is asked whether the nil-rate band rises automatically with inflation each tax year. What should they advise?
options: Yes, it is uprated automatically by the Consumer Prices Index
No, it is a frozen cash figure reviewed periodically by government
Yes, but only for estates above £1 million
No, it was abolished and replaced entirely by the residence nil-rate band
testPool.explanation: The nil-rate band has been held at a fixed cash figure for an extended period and is reviewed periodically rather than automatically uprated — always check the figure current at the relevant date of death.

testPool.prompt: What is the maximum percentage of a predeceasing spouse's unused nil-rate band that can be transferred to a surviving spouse's estate?
testPool.explanation: The transferable NRB is capped at 100% of one NRB, however many previous spouses or civil partners predeceased the survivor — the survivor's estate cannot benefit from more than double the standard NRB in total.

testPool.prompt: For the residence nil-rate band to be available at all, to whom must the qualifying residential interest pass?
options: Any beneficiary named in the will
Direct descendants, such as children or grandchildren
The deceased's spouse only, never children
Any UK-resident individual
testPool.explanation: The RNRB is conditional on the qualifying residence passing to direct descendants — leaving the home to, say, a sibling or a friend does not engage the RNRB at all.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following statements about the spouse exemption is correct?
options: It is capped at £3,000 per tax year, the same as the annual exemption
It is unlimited between UK-domiciled spouses and civil partners
It only applies to gifts made during the couple's lifetime, not on death
It requires HMRC's prior approval before it can be claimed
testPool.trapExplanation: Students sometimes confuse the spouse exemption's unlimited nature with the much smaller £3,000 annual exemption, or assume it is lifetime-only. It applies without limit to both lifetime transfers and transfers on death between UK-domiciled spouses and civil partners, and needs no prior HMRC approval.

testPool.prompt: A donor gives £3,500 to their niece in a tax year in which they made no other gifts and had not used the previous year's annual exemption. How much of that gift, at most, could be covered by the annual exemption alone?
options: £3,000 only, with the remaining £500 potentially chargeable
£6,000, using both this year's and the previous year's unused allowance
£3,500 in full, since any single gift under £5,000 is automatically exempt
Nothing, since the small gifts exemption has already been used
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is stopping at the current year's £3,000 figure. Because one year's unused annual exemption can be carried forward, and none was used the previous year, up to £6,000 is available, covering the full £3,500 gift.

testPool.prompt: A wealthy grandmother gives her grandson £250 for his birthday and, in the same tax year, also gives him £3,000 using her annual exemption. Is the £250 gift separately exempt under the small gifts exemption?
options: Yes, small gifts and the annual exemption can always be combined for the same recipient
No — the small gifts exemption cannot be used for a recipient who already benefits from another exemption in the same tax year
Yes, but only if the £250 is given in cash rather than by bank transfer
No, because the small gifts exemption only applies to gifts to charities
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is assuming exemptions simply stack. Section 20 expressly excludes the small gifts exemption where another exemption has already been used for the same recipient in the same tax year — here, the grandson already benefited from the annual exemption.

testPool.prompt: A widower's estate is worth £2.5 million net, above the RNRB taper threshold, and includes a family home left to his daughter. What is the likely effect on his RNRB?
options: No effect — the taper only applies to estates over £10 million
The RNRB reduces, and may be extinguished entirely, because the estate's net value exceeds the taper threshold
The RNRB automatically doubles for estates over £2 million
The taper only applies if the home itself is worth more than £2 million
testPool.explanation: Once an estate's net value exceeds the taper threshold, the RNRB reduces by £1 for every £2 over that threshold, and for a sufficiently large estate — such as one at £2.5 million — the RNRB can be reduced to nil.

testPool.prompt: A widow's late husband left his entire estate to her under the spouse exemption, using none of his NRB or RNRB. She later dies owning a home left to their children, with an estate comfortably below the RNRB taper threshold. What is available to her estate?
options: Only her own single NRB and single RNRB
Up to double her own NRB and double her own RNRB, both fully transferred from her husband
Double her NRB only — RNRB cannot be transferred between spouses at all
Nothing extra, since transferability only applies to estates that used a will trust
testPool.explanation: Because the husband's whole estate passed to her under the spouse exemption, both his NRB and his RNRB were entirely unused and are available to transfer, giving her estate up to double each band.

testPool.prompt: An elderly man sold his large house four years before his death and moved into rented accommodation, owning no property at death. He left the proceeds of sale to his son and daughter. Can his estate still benefit from an RNRB-related relief?
options: No — since he owned no home at death, no residence-related relief is available
Yes — the downsizing addition can preserve an amount reflecting the RNRB he would have had, since assets of equivalent value passed to his direct descendants
Yes, but only if he had bought a smaller replacement home rather than renting
No — the downsizing addition only applies to gifts made during the seven years before death
testPool.explanation: The downsizing addition exists precisely for this situation: a deceased who sold or gave away a qualifying home and left assets of equivalent value to direct descendants does not simply lose the RNRB because no residence exists at the date of death.

testPool.prompt: A retired teacher makes regular monthly payments to her grandson from her pension income, leaving her standard of living unaffected, over several years before her death. Which exemption is most likely to cover these gifts?
options: The annual exemption, because the payments were regular
Normal expenditure out of income
The small gifts exemption, because each payment is modest
No exemption applies to regular payments
testPool.explanation: Regular gifts made out of surplus income, which do not reduce the donor's usual standard of living, fall within the normal expenditure out of income exemption — a distinct and often more valuable relief than the annual or small gifts exemptions for this pattern of giving.

testPool.prompt: Section 23 IHTA 1984 provides an unlimited exemption for gifts to qualifying charities. What further consequence can leaving at least 10% of a net estate to charity have?
options: It has no further effect beyond exempting the charitable gift itself
It can reduce the rate of inheritance tax charged on the rest of the estate
It automatically exempts the whole estate from inheritance tax
It disqualifies the estate from using the residence nil-rate band
testPool.explanation: Beyond the unlimited exemption on the charitable gift itself, leaving at least 10% of a qualifying net estate to charity can reduce the rate applied to the remainder of the taxable estate.

testPool.prompt: A father gives £250 each to five grandchildren in the same tax year, using no other exemption for any of them. How is this treated under the small gifts exemption?
options: It is not exempt at all, because the total exceeds £250
Each £250 gift is separately exempt, since the £250 limit applies per recipient, not per donor's total giving
Only the first two gifts are exempt, with the rest chargeable
The gifts are exempt only if made in a single combined payment
testPool.explanation: The small gifts exemption operates per recipient per tax year, not as a cap on the donor's total giving — five separate gifts of £250, one to each grandchild, can each be fully exempt.

testPool.prompt: Which statutory provision governs the downsizing addition, preserving RNRB where a qualifying home has been sold before death?
options: Inheritance Tax Act 1984, s 8FE
Inheritance Tax Act 1984, s 18
Trustee Act 1925, s 27
Finance Act 1986, s 102
testPool.explanation: The downsizing addition provisions sit within s 8FA-8FE IHTA 1984, addressing estates where a qualifying home was sold, given away, or otherwise ceased to be owned before death.

testPool.prompt: A student states that the residence nil-rate band applies automatically to any home in an estate, regardless of who inherits it. Is this correct?
options: Yes, the RNRB applies to any residential property in the estate
No — the RNRB only applies where a qualifying residential interest passes to direct descendants
Yes, provided the home is the deceased's only property
No, the RNRB was abolished and replaced by the transferable NRB
testPool.trapExplanation: The RNRB is not a general property relief — it is conditional on the residence passing to direct descendants. A home left to a friend, sibling, or unrelated beneficiary does not engage it, however clearly it is the deceased's residence.

testPool.prompt: An estate is worth £900,000 net, comfortably below the RNRB taper threshold, and includes a home worth £300,000 left equally to the deceased's two children, alongside other assets. The deceased had no transferred NRB or RNRB available. What best describes the tax-free threshold likely available?
options: Only the standard NRB, since the home falls outside any additional relief
The standard NRB plus the RNRB, since a qualifying home passes to direct descendants and the estate is well under the taper threshold
Only the RNRB, since the standard NRB is used up first by other assets
No tax-free threshold at all, because the estate exceeds £500,000
testPool.explanation: With the home passing to the deceased's children and the estate's net value well below the taper threshold, both the standard NRB and the RNRB are available in full, giving a combined tax-free threshold before any exemptions are even applied.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap in this lesson is treating the RNRB as unconditional, or forgetting that its taper is measured against the whole estate's net value rather than the home alone. A close second is assuming exemptions simply stack without checking whether one excludes another, as with small gifts and the annual exemption for the same recipient.
